bandReport.notes:
Band d = items 51-80 (30 items), the LAST band of the paper. Item 80 is the final item of the booklet; p42 ends with it and nothing follows. Item 51 opens cleanly under a fresh 'Directions for the following 2 (two) items' block at the top of p32, so the band does not open mid-item.

PASSAGES / SETS (3 directions blocks, 5 passages, 7 comprehension items):
- p32, 'Directions for the following 2 (two) items' over TWO passages: Passage-1 governs item 51 ONLY; Passage-2 governs item 52 ONLY. Two single-item passages, not one shared 2-item set.
- p36, 'Directions for the following 2 (two) items' over TWO passages: Passage-1 governs item 61 ONLY; Passage-2 governs item 62 ONLY. Again two single-item passages.
- p40, 'Directions for the following 3 (three) items' over TWO passages: Passage-1 (Silk Road / resource extraction) governs item 71 ONLY; Passage-2 (deliberate lies / semantic lies) governs items 72 AND 73. This is the band's ONLY genuine multi-item set. The context strings for 72 and 73 were written once and copied, so they are byte-identical including the curly quotes and the six-dot ellipsis.
Assignment was checked against item content, not just page position: 71 says 'best sums up the passage given above' directly under Passage-1; 72 asks about 'the first part of the passage' (the agreement-about-lies opening of Passage-2); 73 asks about habits of good people (the semantic-lies closing of Passage-2).

DECIMAL SEPARATOR: NOT DETERMINABLE FROM THIS BAND — there is no decimal fraction anywhere in items 51-80. Nothing to report either way. What I can say is that every full stop I did see is an ordinary baseline period, never a raised middle dot: sentence periods throughout, and the ellipsis in item 79's '(1111...)' which I zoomed to check specifically because it was the closest glyph in the band to a decimal point. Large numbers in the band (30000 in item 66; 1000/10000/100000/1000000 in item 68; 15713 etc. in item 79) are printed with NO thousands separator at all, so they give no evidence either. Item 80's '7/8' is a printed fraction, not a decimal.

PRINTED DEFECTS, transcribed verbatim and NOT corrected:
- Item 62 (p36) Passage-2 opens 'In our schools; we teach our children' — a SEMICOLON after 'schools' where a comma belongs. Zoomed to 2.6x to confirm it is a semicolon (dot above, comma tail below) and not a comma with a scan speck. Preserved as printed.
- Item 55 (p34) reads '...then Y will have half of as much as Z...' — 'half of as much as' is awkward/garbled but is what is printed. Zoomed to confirm. Preserved. This wording makes the intended relation genuinely ambiguous; flagged so the blind pass is aware the stem, not the reader, is the difficulty.

TYPOGRAPHY NORMALISED (content unchanged):
- Item 65 options are printed with wide decorative letter-spacing ('b a b a b a'); transcribed as the plain 6-character strings 'bababa', 'baabba', 'bbaabb', 'ababab'. Each is 6 characters, matching the six blanks.
- Item 75 prints 5th/24th/9th and item 71's passage prints 15th with a superscript 'th'; transcribed as plain '5th', '24th', '9th', '15th', matching the convention in the already-shipped p2 files.
- Item 65's series is '_b_a_ba_b_abab_aab' — zoomed to 2.4x and counted: exactly six underscores, matching the stated 'six blanks'. Underscores left bare and unescaped, matching the shipped convention for sequence items.

COLUMN CROPS: all 6 pages read cleanly from the c1/c2 crops; no page needed to be read off the full-page image. The crops are slightly generous rather than sliced — p34-c1 and p38-c1 each carry a sliver of the next column's item numbers ('57.'/'58.' and '68.'/'69.'/'70.') at their right edge, but every one of those items also appears complete at the left edge of its own c2 crop, so nothing was lost or double-counted. Full-page p42.png was additionally checked to confirm nothing spans the gutter and that item 80 closes the paper.

No item number is missing or repeated in 51-80; every item has exactly 4 options.

questions.context: The best universities like Harvard and MIT, despite having the luxury of having some truly excellent teachers on their payroll, are increasingly embracing the “flipped classroom” format, where students listen to video lectures at home, and spend class time applying their knowledge, solving problems, discussing examples, etc. Professors guide that discussion and fill in wherever necessary, explaining those bits that seem to be eluding the students and throwing in advanced ideas that happen to be topical. These universities have made their video lectures available free for anyone in the world. They are also encouraging colleges and universities all over the world to integrate these online courses into their own pedagogy, picking the pieces that are appropriate for their needs and building a package around them.

Our cities contribute to 65 per cent of the GDP, but there are not enough facilities to cater to the needs of the people. It is important to address the issues of air quality, transport, etc., that are vital to identifying sustainable solutions. We need to involve citizens in city planning and create an ecosystem that meets the needs of the people.

questions.context: Can a democracy avoid being a welfare state for long ? Why cannot mass welfare be left entirely to the markets ? There is a built-in tension between markets and democracy. Markets do not work on a one-person-one-vote principle as democracies do. What one gets out of the market place depends on one’s endowments, skills, purchasing power and the forces of demand and supply. Markets reward individual initiative and skill, and may also lift many from the bottom rungs of society, but some people never get the opportunity to develop skills that markets demand; they are simply too poor and too handicapped; or skill formation takes too long. By creating jobs, markets may be able to help even unskilled people, but capitalism has always witnessed bursts of unemployment.
questions.stem:
With reference to the above passage, the following assumptions have been made :
1. Modern democracies rely on the market forces to enable them to be welfare states.
2. Markets ensure sufficient economic growth necessary for democracies to be effective.
3. Government programmes are needed for those left behind in economic growth.
Which of the above assumptions is/are valid ?

questions.context: In our schools; we teach our children all that is there to know about physics, maths and history and what-have-you. But do we teach them about the bitter caste divide that plagues the country, about the spectre of famine that stalks large parts of our land, about gender sensitivity, about the possibility of atheism as a choice, etc. ? Equally important, do we teach them to ask questions, or do we teach them only to passively receive our wisdom ? From the cocooned world of school, suddenly, the adolescent finds himself/herself in the unfettered world of university. Here he/she is swept up in a turmoil of ideas, influences and ideologies. For someone who has been discouraged from asking questions and forming an opinion, this transition can be painful.
